Q: How to persuade browsers on a local network to treat a locally delivered web app like it was on a live site? A:

Host your test site in a hosting service and use a Let's Encrypt free SSL/TLS certificate. Those are already recognized by browsers on modern versions of Android.

Q: AWS-cloudformation: Resource handler returned message: "An ARN in the specified key policy is invalid. " A:

Instead of

            Principal:
              AWS: arn:aws:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:root

it should be

            Principal:
              AWS: !Sub "arn:aws:iam::${AWS::AccountId}:root"

Q: Does std::atomic remain atomic when a struct is allocated with malloc? A:

@Juliean answered the language-lawyer version of the question, about what the standard says.

Practically, the concerns are alignment, and running the constructor to init a mutex inside the atomic object if it's non-lock-free and the implementation works that way.

On most normal implementations, it's almost certain that alignof(std::atomic<int64_t>) is less than or equal to alignof(max_align_t) (https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/types/max_align_t.html), so a malloc large enough to hold it will also be aligned enough for atomic. A possible exception to this would be a 32-bit or narrower system which doesn't have any standard types which get more than 4-byte alignment, but which can do lock-free atomics on aligned 8-byte objects, and that's what std::atomic uses.

static_assert(alignof(Foo) <= alignof(std::max_align_t), "malloc isn't aligned enough for atomic<int64_t>");

If std::atomic<int64_t> isn't lock-free (e.g. on some 32-bit or narrower systems), and the implementation keeps a mutex or other lock in the std::atomic object itself (like MSVC does), then the constructor needs to run. Use placement-new to construct the std::atomic object.
(Or of course use new instead of malloc to allocate the object, but lets say you're writing your own allocator and carving up a large buffer into chunks, as in What uses are there for "placement new"?)

    auto p = static_cast<Foo*>(std::malloc(sizeof(Foo)));
    // placement-new the whole struct
    new (p) Foo();  // or Foo{1,2} to give non-zero values for the struct members

Or just init the atomic member and leave the age uninitialized if that's what you want.

    new (p->value) std::int64_t();   // instead of the whole struct.

In C, I think this is where you'd use atomic_init. The same function exists in C++ to init a default-constructed (i.e. uninitialized) atomic, but is deprecated since C++20, I think because placement-new does the same job. And because C++20 doesn't let you leave an atomic local variable uninitialized; std::atomic_int foo; is the same as std::atomic_int foo(0); in C++20 and later.

In practice, if std::atomic<int64_t>'s object-representation is just a bare int64_t, it will happen to work fine without new. There are no trap-representations for int64_t (it's required to be 64-bit 2's complement on implementations that support it.) This is the case on most mainstream 64-bit implementations, and many 32-bit implementations. The behaviour is still undefined by the C++ standard; working the way you expect is one possible outcome, which makes C++ harder to test for portability than some languages.

Godbolt showing GCC targeting x86-64 and MSVC targeting 32-bit x86, both with lock-free atomic int64_t. I don't know of any compiler on Godbolt where sizeof(std::atomic<int64_t>) != sizeof(int64_t); 32-bit MSVC for ARM doesn't seem to work, or I don't know the magic command-line options to tell it to build a console instead of desktop application if that's what it wants. Some of the targets have non-lock-free atomic<int64_t>, but GCC and Clang use a separate hash-table of locks rather than embedding one in every atomic object. If you want to see what that looks like, use x86 or x64 MSVC with a larger type, like 32 bytes, like std::atomic<some_struct>. Or maybe an odd size like 5 bytes if it's not willing to pad the object for you.
